blocks.text: Meet Midjourney

Today, we meet a faster way to create powerful visuals and enhance your storytelling with images, keeping it all consistent and appealing. Midjourney is an AI tool that generates images from your written request. That's how your design story begins: without complex software, without brushes — just prompts!
How Does It Work?
You can use Midjourney in two main ways:

• In the Midjourney web app, where you type your prompt into the "Imagine" bar
  • On Discord, where you talk to the Midjourney Bot with commands
In this course, we'll focus on the web app, which offers a cleaner interface, visual settings, and organized workspaces.

blocks.template: A beautiful [subject] [setting]

blocks.text: Great Job!

See? The way you get results from the tool is simple: you describe what you want — Midjourney creates stunning art from your words. Whether it's social media content, product concepts, or digital illustration, the tool has you covered!
Navigating the Interface

When you open Midjourney, you'll see the "Imagine" bar above — this is where you type your prompts, like the one you just created. In the "Explore" tab, you'll find the works of other users to get inspired, and in the "Create" tab — your own art.
As you've already noticed, once you enter your request, Midjourney gives you four options at a time. It's like having four artists paint your idea simultaneously!
Editing Your Result

Let's say you've actually generated four sunset pictures. They are okay, but not exactly what you wanted. 

Once you hover over any of them, you'll see buttons for quick changes:

• "Vary Subtle" — creates a variation of the selected image that stays very close to the original
  • "Vary Strong" — larger changes in composition, shape, style, or mood
  • "Animate" — generates a short animation based on the image
You can find the same commands and even more if you click on any image in the bottom right corner.
Creation Actions
You can use this panel to set up and control:

• Image variations — create subtle or stronger alternate versions without changing the core idea.
  • Upscaling — increase resolution and detail, either conservatively or with a more creative touch.
  • Reruns and edits — regenerate the image or make targeted adjustments without rewriting everything.
  • Reuse options — apply the same image, style, or prompt as a starting point for a new generation.
Animation settings:

• Motion intensity — choose between low or high movement for calmer loops or more dynamic results.
  • Loop behavior — control how the animation repeats for a seamless or expressive effect.
There are even more customization and modification capabilities in Midjourney — we will learn more about them in future lessons!
However, you don't just make changes by hitting buttons in this tool. Great art starts with even greater prompts!
The Importance of Prompts
Prompts are the way of telling AI exactly what you want: subject, mood, lighting, style, even camera angle. Change one word, and your image can go from "okay" to "award-winning" or vice-versa.

Crafting Images with Precision

You've already seen how Midjourney turns simple words into visual stories.

Today, you'll take the next step: learning how the phrasing of your prompt and changes in it can completely reshape your results. Let's discover what makes a good prompt and how to get exactly what you want from the tool!
Choosing the Right Words

Suppose you are creating an illustrated book of fairytales that you can later sell online or give as a gift to children. The text goes: "A tall castle rises above the valley as the sun begins to climb." You want to show the valley and the skyscraping castle towers. The image should feel dramatic, magical, and full of height.

feedbackCorrect.text: "Towering" activates a very different visual pattern than "gigantic" or "big." It signals height, drama, and vertical emphasis, guiding Midjourney toward a more striking composition.

feedbackIncorrect.text: "Big" is too generic and can be interpreted as wide, bulky, or simply large — it doesn't guarantee a dramatic silhouette. "Gigantic" doesn't work because it adds width rather than height.

blocks.prompt: Decide which word creates the intended visual effect, then fix the prompt.
blocks.template: A [big] castle on a cliff at sunrise
blocks.title: How Much Does One Word Change?

blocks.text: The words you use guide the image. Specific terms give Midjourney a clearer direction. Instead of "beautiful," try "elegant," "serene," or "vibrant." Instead of "fast," try "swift" or "racing." Sharper wording leads to more intentional results.
blocks.title: 💡 First Discovery: Choose Precise Language

blocks.text: Use Exact Quantities
Another tip for clarity in your prompts: avoid vague plurals.

• "flowers" → open to interpretation
  • "twelve flowers arranged in a circle" → clear composition
You can also use collective terms like "a cluster of lanterns" instead of simply "lanterns."
More Prompting Pitfalls

Let's now look at some more tricky parts that might affect your result.

Imagine you are preparing a productivity guideline for your team and need a clean workspace shot. You want something tidy, simple, and visually calm.

feedbackCorrect.text: Positive, specific instructions tell Midjourney exactly what to include, reducing ambiguity and avoiding unintended shapes.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Negative or vague phrasing like "no clutter" or "nothing unnecessary" still activates clutter-like concepts and leaves room for interpretation!

options.label: clean, minimal design with one laptop and soft lighting

blocks.prompt: Twist the prompt so Midjourney produces the desired result.
blocks.template: A desk setup with [no clutter]
blocks.title: From Pitfall to Clarity

blocks.text: Negative instructions can still introduce the thing you're trying to avoid. Like we just saw, if you write "a desk setup with no clutter," you may still see clutter-like shapes. Focus instead on what should appear: "a clean, minimal desk setup with one laptop and soft lighting."
blocks.title: 💡 Second Discovery: Describe What You Want

blocks.text: For removing elements, add the "--no" parameter at the end of your request to exclude items explicitly. For example, "--no text," "--no people," or "--no clouds" tells Midjourney to avoid adding those items. It's not perfect — the model may still include subtle traces of the excluded object — but it's the most reliable way to reduce unwanted details.
blocks.title: Pro Tip

blocks.text: For example, here is how the "--no" parameter works in our clean desk setup request: "A desk setup --no clutter" We will explore more parameters in future lessons!

You don't always need many details in your prompts: they can stay minimal — even a couple of words or emojis work. When you keep things short, Midjourney relies more on its default style to complete the image.
If certain elements matter to you, include them. The fewer details you specify, the more variety you get, but you also lose control over the final result.

Be clear about details that matter to you. Parts to consider:
  • Subject: Who or what? (person, animal, character, location, object)
  • Medium: In what form? (digital photo, oil painting, illustration, sculpture, charcoal sketch)
  • Environment: Where? (indoors, outdoors, in outer space, underwater, in the city)
  • Lighting: What kind? (golden hour, soft candlelight, dramatic, neon)
  • Color: In what shades? (muted, pastel, bold primary colors, warm tones, grayscale, monochromatic, black and white)
  • Mood: Feelings to evoke? (energetic, dreamy, mysterious, cheerful)
  • Composition: How is it framed? (portrait, wide shot, macro close-up, birds-eye view)

To get straight to the point, you need to include all important details — but you should do it the right way.

Imagine you want to build an illustrated wildlife guide for junior schoolchildren. You need to show a baby deer lying safely while two bluebirds watch from a branch above — soft forest morning light, gentle cartoonish style.

blocks.text: Why This Works
This prompt works because each detail reinforces a calm, child-friendly illustration:

• Clear subject: the baby deer is the focus.
  • Defined relationship: bluebirds above → no blending or confusion.
  • Simple environment: forest clearing keeps the scene readable.
  • Unified style: soft cartoon look matches the gentle tone.
  • Consistent mood: morning light adds warmth.
  • Single viewpoint: wide-shot keeps all elements in frame naturally.
Together, these choices guide Midjourney toward a clean, coherent result.

Your prompt only works if all its parts agree with each other. When you mix conflicting details, like opposite styles or impossible viewpoints, Midjourney tries to satisfy everything at once. The result is often blurred, blended, or surreal. A coherent prompt is not about adding more information — it's about adding the right information that supports a single, unified picture.
blocks.title: 💡 Third Discovery: Add Details Wisely

blocks.text: From Words to Visual Control

Prompting isn't about crowding the prompt with details — it’s about making purposeful choices. 

Whether you're illustrating stories, designing products, or creating visuals for fun, the same rules apply: choose the right words, add the right details, and keep everything aligned.

• Choose precise language. Sharp, specific words steer the model toward accurate shapes, proportions, and mood.
  • Describe what you want: positive instructions outperform negative ones. Tell Midjourney what should appear — not what shouldn't.
  • Add details wisely. Your prompt must speak with one voice. Avoid conflicting, unclear, or impossible descriptions.
Together, these principles give you real control over your images and help Midjourney bring your ideas to life with clarity and intention.

These fundamentals give you real control and help Midjourney understand the story you're trying to tell.

Transform Your AI Art with Lighting

Imagine this: you enter Midjourney with a strong subject in mind, but the output feels flat. The shapes are there, yet the emotion is missing. Often, the missing ingredient is lighting — the element that quietly controls depth, mood, and realism. Today, you'll explore how small lighting choices change the story your image tells.
Lighting isn't just about brightness — it's what shapes emotion and focus. Let's look at how direction, shadows, and intensity help your images tell a story, step by step.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right, the side light is meant to add some dramatic effect to the image. Let's see how the atmosphere changes if we try another direction.

blocks.template: [Subject] with flowers in her hair [action] with [lighting direction]

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! Front light typically softens features — dramatic effect is low, the subject looks clear and bright.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Actually, what changed is how soft the images are — dramatic effect is low, the subject looks clear and bright.

blocks.question: What changes did you notice this time?

blocks.text: See? Even small shifts in the direction of light can completely change the focus and emotion.

Front light:
  • Even illumination with minimal shadows
  • Creates a clean, clear, low-drama look
Side light:
  • Adds shadows, contrast, and depth
  • Creates a more dramatic, textured feel
Backlight:
  • Produces glow or silhouette effects
  • Adds atmosphere and separates subject from background

blocks.text: Using Shadows

Shadows reveal structure and balance — and without them, even the best composition feels flat. 

Try changing the shadow length or contrast to see how the mood transforms!

blocks.prompt: Add shadow effects to your image.
blocks.template: [Subject] [action] with [shadow effect]

blocks.prompt: Now, experiment with varying shadow effects in your image.
blocks.template: [Subject] [action] with [shadow effect]

feedbackCorrect.text: Right! Short soft shadows make the image feel gentle, natural, and low-contrast, with minimal drama.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Actually, long sharp shadows create strong contrast, adding depth and drama.

blocks.question: Which group of images feels more gentle and natural?

blocks.text:
Soft shadows:
  • Created by large, diffused light (cloudy sky, softbox, indirect light)
  • Make the image feel gentle, natural, and low-contrast
Sharp shadows:
  • Created by small, direct light (sunlight, spotlight)
  • Add strong contrast, drama, and crisp definition
blocks.title: Shadow Contrast Cheat Sheet

blocks.text:
Short shadows:
  • Light comes from high above
  • Creates a clean, bright look with minimal mood or drama
Long shadows:
  • Light comes from low on the horizon
  • Adds depth, direction, and a dramatic or cinematic feel
blocks.title: Shadow Length Cheat Sheet

blocks.text: Experimenting with Intensity

As your next step, consider the intensity of the light — it changes mood faster than any filter!

Too strong, and you lose detail. Too dim, and you lose the story.
Test everything — harsh sunlight, foggy dusk, candlelight glow. You'll see how brightness shifts emotion from warm and welcoming to eerie or powerful.

blocks.template: [Subject] in [light intensity]

blocks.prompt: Twist the intensity of light in your image.
blocks.template: [Subject] in [light intensity]

blocks.text: Practicing with Lighting Effects
Ready to put it all together? Let's combine what you've learned — direction, shadows, and intensity.

blocks.prompt: Create an image with a set of lighting effects.
blocks.template: [Subject] [time of day] with [shadow length] on the ground as the orange sun shines [light direction]

blocks.text: Refining Your Lighting Prompts

See what we did there?

We didn't define the light intensity explicitly, but we mentioned the time of day, and Midjourney made the light intensity appear like it would at sunset.
You can actually describe lighting without even using the word "light" — "during the sunset" says a lot already. Think "under neon signs," "golden hour portrait," "misty forest at dawn."
blocks.title: Pro Tip

feedbackCorrect.text: Describing lighting through mood, natural cues like "sunset," or by combining shadow, direction, and intensity helps the AI create more nuanced and visually cohesive images.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Relying entirely on AI creativity or skipping light cues often results in unpredictable or flat outcomes. Even indirect mentions like "dawn" or "foggy" guide Midjourney more effectively!

blocks.hint: Think about what influences how Midjourney interprets your scene, even without directly using the word "light."

  • Intensity sets the tone: bright light feels open and confident; dim or diffused light feels moody or mysterious.
  • You don't need the word "light." Cues like "sunset," "candlelight," or "misty forest at dawn" tell Midjourney everything it needs to know.

Too strong, and you lose detail. Too dim, and you lose the story.

blocks.text: Practicing with Lighting Effects
Ready to put it all together? Let's combine what you've learned — direction, shadows, and intensity.

blocks.prompt: Create an image with a set of lighting effects.
blocks.template: [Subject] [time of day] with [shadow length] on the ground as the orange sun shines [light direction]

blocks.text: Refining Your Lighting Prompts

See what we did there?

We didn't define the light intensity explicitly, but we mentioned the time of day, and Midjourney made the light intensity appear like it would at sunset.
You can actually describe lighting without even using the word "light" — "during the sunset" says a lot already. Think "under neon signs," "golden hour portrait," "misty forest at dawn."

Why Image Size Matters
Image size in Midjourney isn't just a technical detail — it's the foundation of your entire scene.

When you choose an image size in Midjourney, you're actually choosing the aspect ratio — the relationship between width and height. It shapes how much of a scene fits into the frame, how your composition flows, and even how the viewer reads the image.
How Aspect Ratios Work in Midjourney
Midjourney lets you define aspect ratios in two ways:

1. Through the "Image Size" setting in the interface (which adjusts the aspect ratio automatically).
  2. By adding the "--ar" parameter at the end of your prompt — for example: --ar 3:2.
Both methods tell Midjourney exactly how the frame should be shaped before anything else is generated.

Direct the Camera, Shape the Story

Welcome back! Today, you'll learn how to guide Midjourney by choosing the viewpoint — the angle and distance from which your scene is observed. This single choice can turn a simple image into something dramatic, intimate, or cinematic. Let's explore how positioning the "camera" transforms your results!
Why View Matters
Viewpoint tells Midjourney where the viewer stands in the scene.

• A low angle makes subjects feel powerful
  • A high angle makes them feel small or cinematic
  • A close viewpoint pulls the viewer into the moment
  • A distant one builds context and space
By choosing the viewpoint intentionally, you control emotion, focus, and narrative.
Setting View in Your Prompt
You can guide Midjourney by indicating the camera position directly in your prompt:

• "from a low angle"
  • "bird's-eye view"
  • "eye level"
  • "close-up portrait"
  • "wide shot from a distance"
These cues help the model frame your subject with purpose, instead of relying on its default perspective.

blocks.text: Direct the Camera, Shape the Story

Welcome back! Today, you'll learn how to guide Midjourney by choosing the viewpoint — the angle and distance from which your scene is observed. This single choice can turn a simple image into something dramatic, intimate, or cinematic. Let's explore how positioning the "camera" transforms your results!
Why View Matters
Viewpoint tells Midjourney where the viewer stands in the scene.

• A low angle makes subjects feel powerful
  • A high angle makes them feel small or cinematic
  • A close viewpoint pulls the viewer into the moment
  • A distant one builds context and space
By choosing the viewpoint intentionally, you control emotion, focus, and narrative.
Setting View in Your Prompt
You can guide Midjourney by indicating the camera position directly in your prompt:

• "from a low angle"
  • "bird's-eye view"
  • "eye level"
  • "close-up portrait"
  • "wide shot from a distance"
These cues help the model frame your subject with purpose, instead of relying on its default perspective.
Practicing with Viewpoints

Remember your client from the previous lesson? They absolutely loved the images you created for their website and social media! Now, with the holiday season approaching, they want you to design postcards their guests can send home. The postcards should feel like a painting of the resort — warm, inviting, and showing how cozy the houses look nestled between snowy mountain peaks.

Fine-Tune Your Visual Direction

Welcome to the second unit — where you begin shaping not only what Midjourney creates, but how it looks. Today's focus is style — the part that influences clarity, mood, and communication. Understanding how style works helps you move from experimenting at random to producing images that feel consistent and intentional.
Exploring Style

You already shaped images using parameters like --ar for framing and --no for exclusions. Those tools helped you control structure. Another thing that parameters can set is style — but it adds another layer. It affects texture, contrast, detail, and atmosphere — the qualities that shape how a viewer reads your scene. Exploring these elements gives you more control over the final result.
Style as a Combination of Cues
A style is built from several visible elements working together, such as:

• Color — soft, bold, muted, or bright
  • Texture — smooth, grainy, painterly
  • Contrast — strong or subtle
  • Shapes — geometric or organic
  • Detail level — minimal or intricate
Noticing these cues helps you describe and refine style more easily.
Why Prompt Phrasing Isn't Always Enough

Throughout the lessons, you've already tried adding phrases like "watercolor style" or "cartoonish" to your prompts. Let's see how such descriptions guide Midjourney.

Say you want to design a holiday poster for your office that conveys the festive atmosphere. You imagine it in traditional Christmas holiday colors.

blocks.text: Meet Personalize

Midjourney has a feature that solves exactly this kind of problem. It's called Personalize, and it works like a style memory — you teach Midjourney what you like, and it applies that to every image you generate. You'll find it as a small "P" pill next to the search bar, with an On/Off toggle.
There are two ways to teach Midjourney your style:

• Rate images: Midjourney shows you visuals, you pick the ones you like, and it learns your taste over time. This builds a Profile.
  • Upload references: you gather images you already love into a Moodboard, and Midjourney studies them.
Both shape the same parameter: "--p". When Personalize is turned on, Midjourney adds it to your prompts.
Let Midjourney Learn by Rating

When you first open the Personalize panel, you'll see your Global Profile — it's there by default, waiting to be unlocked. To unlock it, click "Rate More Images." Midjourney shows you a grid, and you pick the visuals that match your taste. The more you rate, the more your Global Profile sharpens.
Create Multiple Profiles

One Profile isn't always enough. You might work on different projects — a calm wellness brand one week, a bold sports campaign the next. For cases like this, you can click "Create Profile" to build a separate one. Each new Profile is trained the same way — by rating images — but remains independent.
Profiles work well when you want Midjourney to learn your taste gradually.
But sometimes you have a specific look in mind right now, and references already in hand. Here comes another cool feature — Moodboards.
Personalize from References
Moodboards allow you to gather references and observe patterns across examples. Researching different visual directions and then showing them to Midjourney helps a lot with defining style.

You gather a few winter-themed images and place them into a moodboard. After you've uploaded your images, click "Use in Prompt" — Midjourney will create a "--p" parameter with a unique number that personalizes your prompt. Then, you request whatever you want to see — the image will be similar in style and vibe to the moodboard.

feedbackCorrect.text: Moodboards influence the visual style of an image — things like color palette, texture, and overall rendering. These elements tend to stay consistent across results when a moodboard is applied.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Moodboards don't introduce new subjects or lock images into the same composition. They guide how the image looks, not what appears in the scene or how it's arranged.

blocks.text: What Moodboards Reveal

See? You don't even need to mention colors. Moodboards help you notice which elements repeat across your references — colors, shapes, textures, or lighting patterns. These shared cues form the style direction your images follow.
Style Creator
Profiles and Moodboards both assume you already know what you like. But what if you don't? That's where Style Creator comes in.
Creating a Style Through Iteration
The Style Creator doesn't start with finished references. Instead, it helps you discover a style by iterating on your own prompt. Let's dive deeper into it!

You begin by writing a regular prompt — focusing on subject and idea, not style perfection. After you submit your prompt, Midjourney generates a grid of different styles for the same idea. Each option explores a different visual direction. Your task is simple: pick the versions that feel closest to what you want. You're not naming the style — you're reacting to it visually.

With each selection, Midjourney refines the style based on your choices.

After a few rounds, the results begin to stabilize — the colors, textures, and rendering start to feel consistent. At this point, you're no longer browsing styles, but shaping one.
Once you see what you like, you can stop selecting and enjoy the result!
From Direction to Nuance

Early iterations define the overall direction. Later ones refine details.

Roughly:

• The first few rounds establish the style
  • The next several add clarity and consistency
  • Later iterations focus on subtle differences
This process turns preference into a repeatable visual style.
Applying Your Custom Style

Once the style feels right, you can use it in new prompts. Click on it in the right column next to your prompt — it will convert into "--sref" (style reference) parameter and appear in the "Imagine" bar. The subject may change, but the visual treatment stays aligned with the style you shaped. This makes Style Creator especially useful when you want a consistent look without manually adjusting multiple parameters!

blocks.text: Meet Personalize

Midjourney has a feature that solves exactly this kind of problem. It's called Personalize, and it works like a style memory — you teach Midjourney what you like, and it applies that to every image you generate. You'll find it as a small "P" pill next to the search bar, with an On/Off toggle.
There are two ways to teach Midjourney your style:

• Rate images: Midjourney shows you visuals, you pick the ones you like, and it learns your taste over time. This builds a Profile.
  • Upload references: you gather images you already love into a Moodboard, and Midjourney studies them.
Both shape the same parameter: "--p". When Personalize is turned on, Midjourney adds it to your prompts.
Let Midjourney Learn by Rating

When you first open the Personalize panel, you'll see your Global Profile — it's there by default, waiting to be unlocked. To unlock it, click "Rate More Images." Midjourney shows you a grid, and you pick the visuals that match your taste. The more you rate, the more your Global Profile sharpens.
Create Multiple Profiles

One Profile isn't always enough. You might work on different projects — a calm wellness brand one week, a bold sports campaign the next. For cases like this, you can click "Create Profile" to build a separate one. Each new Profile is trained the same way — by rating images — but remains independent.
Profiles work well when you want Midjourney to learn your taste gradually.
But sometimes you have a specific look in mind right now, and references already in hand. Here comes another cool feature — Moodboards.
Personalize from References
Moodboards allow you to gather references and observe patterns across examples. Researching different visual directions and then showing them to Midjourney helps a lot with defining style.

You gather a few winter-themed images and place them into a moodboard. After you've uploaded your images, click "Use in Prompt" — Midjourney will create a "--p" parameter with a unique number that personalizes your prompt. Then, you request whatever you want to see — the image will be similar in style and vibe to the moodboard.

blocks.text: What Moodboards Reveal

See? You don't even need to mention colors. Moodboards help you notice which elements repeat across your references — colors, shapes, textures, or lighting patterns. These shared cues form the style direction your images follow.
Style Creator
Profiles and Moodboards both assume you already know what you like. But what if you don't? That's where Style Creator comes in.
Creating a Style Through Iteration
The Style Creator doesn't start with finished references. Instead, it helps you discover a style by iterating on your own prompt. Let's dive deeper into it!

You begin by writing a regular prompt — focusing on subject and idea, not style perfection. After you submit your prompt, Midjourney generates a grid of different styles for the same idea. Each option explores a different visual direction. Your task is simple: pick the versions that feel closest to what you want. You're not naming the style — you're reacting to it visually.

With each selection, Midjourney refines the style based on your choices.

After a few rounds, the results begin to stabilize — the colors, textures, and rendering start to feel consistent. At this point, you're no longer browsing styles, but shaping one.
Once you see what you like, you can stop selecting and enjoy the result!
From Direction to Nuance

Early iterations define the overall direction. Later ones refine details.

Roughly:

• The first few rounds establish the style
  • The next several add clarity and consistency
  • Later iterations focus on subtle differences
This process turns preference into a repeatable visual style.
Applying Your Custom Style

Once the style feels right, you can use it in new prompts. Click on it in the right column next to your prompt — it will convert into "--sref" (style reference) parameter and appear in the "Imagine" bar. The subject may change, but the visual treatment stays aligned with the style you shaped. This makes Style Creator especially useful when you want a consistent look without manually adjusting multiple parameters!

blocks.text: Good Job!

What's Coming Next

The style awareness you built here will make those controls easier to understand and apply.
Controlling Style With Parameters

Earlier, you explored style visually — comparing directions, noticing patterns, and shaping a look through Moodboards and Style Creator. Now it's time to take the next step! Today, you'll be diving into fine-tuning and customizing your images with style parameters until they look exactly as you imagined. Let's make you handle complex edits easily!
How Style Parameters Work
Style parameters don't change what appears in your image. They change how Midjourney renders it.

Each parameter controls a specific aspect of interpretation — realism, variation, experimentation, or consistency. 

By adjusting them one by one, you learn how to shape results intentionally instead of guessing.

From Adjustments to Decisions

Up to this point, you've learned how individual parameters behave. You've adjusted them, compared results, and seen clear cause-and-effect changes. In real projects, however, you rarely tweak one parameter in isolation. You make decisions under constraints — balancing consistency, expression, clarity, and delivery requirements at the same time. This lesson is about building style systems: parameter setups that solve real creative problems reliably.
A Shift in Thinking
In earlier lessons, the question was simple: What does this control do? Now the question changes:

• What is the goal?
  • What must stay consistent?
  • Where can variation exist?
  • When does creativity help — and when does it hurt?
You'll work through scenarios where there is no perfect answer — only better or worse tradeoffs.
Scenario: Brand Campaign Carousel

Your men's cosmetics campaign from the previous lesson created a buzz and gained wide attention! 

Now you're hired as a brand designer for a women's hair products campaign. The client needs images for a social carousel, and they used this sample of your work as a style reference.
You can easily reuse it as a style reference in Midjourney with a new prompt, as well as set up how heavily this stylization is applied using the "--sw" parameter.

Generating a Few Images at a Time

You've learned how to shape a single image with intention, combining parameters to hit a specific look, mood, or brief.

Now, let's zoom out. Creative work usually starts with a few directions on the table. Today, you'll learn how to test several visual directions in parallel, saving time, credits, and effort along the way!
The Brief

Let's look at one example.

You're working on visuals for a premium coffee brand. Before settling on one direction, you want to see a few options side by side. Your job is to explore fast and bring back a shortlist worth developing.
Two Ways to Generate

Every Midjourney generation runs at full quality by default — high detail, full credit cost and render time. That's the right mode for final assets, but wrong for early exploration when you don't yet know which direction is the strongest one.
What Draft Mode Changes

Draft Mode generates at a lower resolution and costs roughly 4x less than a standard generation. It shows you enough to judge composition, mood, and color, which is all you need when you're still deciding. Midjourney regularly releases new versions, and the latest ones support Draft Mode. As of now, v8 generates 24 images, and v7 produces the standard 4 visual assets.

To apply the Draft Mode, you simply add the --draft parameter at the end of your prompt. You can also access it from the Explore or Create pages. Click the lightning button near the prompt bar, and you're ready to explore in Draft Mode.
Let's generate your first campaign direction! You were thinking about the cozy Sunday morning at home, so now you want to test how well it matches the premium coffee brand.

When checking out the drafts, you're looking for three things:
  • Does the composition work? Strong composition means the subject is clearly placed and the image has visual hierarchy.
  • Does the mood match the brief? Mood fit means the atmosphere matches the brief: premium, intimate, bold, or whatever you need.
  • Is there something here worth developing further? Brief alignment means you can see a path from this draft to an appropriate deliverable.

blocks.text: Test Multiple Directions at Once

You've tested one direction, but for your brief, it's better to have four. Writing and running four separate prompts is slow — and you're likely to miss combinations you never thought to try. Permutations solve this.
How Permutations Work

Permutations are a Midjourney feature that lets you test several versions of a prompt in a single command. Instead of running four separate prompts, you list the options you want to compare, and Midjourney generates all combinations at once. To use them, add options in curly braces separated by commas: {option A, option B}. You can add more than one combination to the same prompt.

blocks.prompt: Complete the permutation prompt. Fill in the content for each variable to test two moods and two styles.
blocks.template: Single espresso cup, marble café counter at dawn, warm cinematic lighting, {[quiet mood], [bold mood]}, premium coffee brand campaign, {editorial photography style, raw documentary style} [aspect ratio] [draft mode parameter]

blocks.text: Reading the Matrix

Good! Now you have four Draft results. Before picking a direction, look at the spread — how different are the results from each other? 

A good matrix shows you four clearly different starting points. If they cluster together, the matrix is telling you something.
Choosing the Right Variables

The most common mistake with permutations is choosing variables that are too similar. If both options in a variable produce near-identical results, you've just generated variations of the same direction twice.

For example, "Editorial + ritual" and "documentary + energy" feel like variations of the same direction rather than four genuinely different ones.

feedbackCorrect.text: Similar results mean similar variables. "Editorial photography" and "raw documentary" both push Midjourney toward realistic, desaturated photography. The gap between them isn't wide enough to produce a real matrix. The fix is more distinct variables, not more generations.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. Quality isn't the issue — Draft Mode preserves enough to evaluate direction. And loosening the prompt would just produce random variation, not structured exploration. When results cluster together, the variables are the problem.

options.label: The prompt is too specific — removing the subject and setting will give Midjourney more room to vary

The fix is straightforward: swap the variables for options that are further apart. Replace {editorial, documentary} with something that produces a genuinely different visual character — like {editorial photography, painterly illustration} — and run a second Draft pass.

blocks.text: The Winner — and What's Still Wrong

After a second pass with wider variables, one direction pulls clearly ahead: editorial photography, quiet ritual mood, marble counter at dawn. The composition works, the premium feel comes through, and the brief is answered. One problem: the lighting reads too cool and clinical. The brief calls for warmth. Everything else is worth keeping.
Where Remix Comes In
Remix lets you edit the prompt of an existing image before generating the next one. It keeps the composition you liked and applies only the changes you ask for.

To access it, open any image you've created from your Create page. This will bring up the image along with additional controls. Then, locate the Creation Actions panel. Here you'll see the Remix options. If you don't see Remix at first, click More options and enable it by checking the "Remix" box.
Which Option to Use
Remix gives you two options:

• Subtle holds the composition close while your prompt changes take effect. Use it when only one element needs to shift.
  • Strong allows bigger departures. Use it when the concept needs a more significant change.

The Brief

Let's look at one example.

You're working on visuals for a premium coffee brand. Before settling on one direction, you want to see a few options side by side. Your job is to explore fast and bring back a shortlist worth developing.
Two Ways to Generate

Every Midjourney generation runs at full quality by default — high detail, full credit cost and render time. That's the right mode for final assets, but wrong for early exploration when you don't yet know which direction is the strongest one.
What Draft Mode Changes

Draft Mode generates at a lower resolution and costs roughly 4x less than a standard generation. It shows you enough to judge composition, mood, and color, which is all you need when you're still deciding. Midjourney regularly releases new versions, and the latest ones support Draft Mode. As of now, v8 generates 24 images, and v7 produces the standard 4 visual assets.

When Details Sell the Product

Product images are judged differently than any other visuals. They must look clean, intentional, and trustworthy. Every shadow, highlight, and angle affects how the product is perceived — premium or cheap, clear or confusing. In this lesson, you'll learn how to design product images deliberately in Midjourney by combining parameters with the right lighting, composition, and viewpoint choices.

blocks.question: What do you think makes product images powerful?

blocks.text: What Makes a Product Image Work
Strong product images usually share a few qualities:

• The product is easy to read at a glance
  • Lighting highlights form and texture
  • Nothing distracts from the subject
  • The framing feels intentional
Achieving this isn't about adding more words. It's about setting the right constraints.
Think Like a Product Photographer
Before writing the prompt, imagine a real photoshoot. Ask yourself:

• Where is the light coming from?
  • How close is the camera?
  • Is the product centered or staged?
  • What mood should the product communicate?
Your prompt should answer these questions clearly.
Scenario: Premium Skincare Product
You're creating visuals for a premium skincare brand. The images will be used on a website and in ads. The product should feel:

• Clean
  • Modern
  • High-end
We'll start with a safe, controlled setup.

blocks.text: Why Raw Mode Matters for Products
For product images, you usually want less interpretation, not more. Raw mode reduces Midjourney's tendency to:

• Over-stylize
  • Exaggerate colors
  • Add artistic textures
This makes surfaces, edges, and proportions feel more realistic and controlled.
Lighting That Sells
Lighting is one of the most important elements in product photography. In prompts, lighting affects:

• How glossy or matte a product looks
  • How textures appear
  • How premium the image feels

Choosing the Right Viewpoint
Viewpoint controls how the product is perceived. Common product viewpoints include:

• Eye-level → neutral and realistic
  • Slight top-down → clean and commercial
  • Close-up → material and detail focus
Extreme angles often distract unless used intentionally.

blocks.question: When is it appropriate to explore and try different parameter values for product images?

blocks.text: Exploration vs Delivery
You might still explore early on — trying different moods or materials. But once a direction is chosen, product images should be:

• Repeatable
  • Consistent
  • Predictable
That's when tightening parameters matters most.
Designing Product Images with Intent
Strong product images aren't about luck. They come from:

• Intentional lighting
  • Simple composition
  • Clear viewpoint
  • Restrained parameter choices
Once these elements work together, Midjourney behaves like a controlled studio — not a guessing machine.

• Strong product images come from constraints: a clear focal point, controlled lighting, nothing that distracts.
  • Raw mode keeps details clean. It reduces over-stylization, exaggerated colors, and artistic textures.
  • Simple composition wins in product imagery. Center the product, balance the spacing, use "--no props" to exclude distractions.
  • Match viewpoint to purpose. Eye-level for realism, slight top-down for commercial, close-up for detail.
  • Explore early, tighten late. Experiment during ideation, lock parameters once the direction is chosen.

Images That Stop the Scroll

Marketing visuals have a different job than product photos. They don't just show — they interrupt, attract, and persuade. In a feed full of noise, your image has seconds to communicate value, emotion, or curiosity. In this lesson, you'll learn how to design bold, memorable marketing visuals in Midjourney — images built to work in ads, landing pages, and campaigns.
How Marketing Visuals Think Differently
Strong marketing visuals usually prioritize:

• Emotion over realism
  • Contrast over subtlety
  • Clarity of message over detail accuracy
This doesn't mean "chaos." It means intentional exaggeration and clear focus.
Start with the Message, Not the Image
Before writing the prompt, define the purpose:

• What should the viewer feel?
  • What action should they take?
  • What stands out at a glance?
Your prompt should reflect the idea first — visuals support it.
Scenario: Online Ad for a Fitness App

This time, let's suppose you were offered to design visuals for a fitness app ad campaign.

The goal:

• Grab attention in a feed
  • Communicate energy and transformation
  • Feel bold, modern, and motivating
This is not simply a realistic photoshoot, but a message-driven image.

blocks.text: Why Chaos Helps Marketing Visuals
Unlike product images, marketing visuals often benefit from variation and surprise. A moderate chaos value can:

• Introduce unexpected framing
  • Create stronger contrast
  • Make images feel less predictable
This helps visuals stand out in crowded spaces.
Adding Boldness with Weirdness
Weirdness pushes ideas beyond the expected. Used carefully, it can:

• Exaggerate emotion
  • Create striking metaphors
  • Make visuals memorable
For marketing, weirdness should support the message — not confuse it.

blocks.template: Dynamic marketing visual of an athlete mid-motion, bold lighting, high contrast, energetic mood, modern advertising style, dramatic composition --ar 4:5 [weirdness]

feedbackIncorrect.text: Increased weirdness made the images more exaggerated and expressive!

options.label: The visual became more exaggerated and expressive

• Strong directional light
  • Rim light to separate subject from background
  • Dramatic shadows

Marketing visuals often use dynamic composition. Common techniques:

• Off-center framing
  • Diagonal lines
  • Close or low viewpoints
These create motion and intensity.
Designing a Marketing Visual System
Strong marketing visuals often combine:

• Expressive prompts
  • Higher chaos for variation
  • Controlled weirdness for memorability
  • Dramatic lighting and angles
Together, these create impact without randomness.

feedbackCorrect.text: The more risk you take, the better the result!

blocks.text: Designing for Impact

Powerful marketing visuals don't aim to be subtle. They are designed to stand out, communicate fast, and trigger emotion. By combining the right parameters with intentional lighting, composition, and viewpoint, you turn Midjourney into a marketing design tool, not just an image generator.

• Marketing visuals are message-driven. They prioritize emotion, contrast, and clarity over realism.

  • Chaos ("--c") stops the scroll. Moderate values add unexpected framing and stronger contrast.

  • Lighting and viewpoint guide the eye. Rim light, dramatic shadows, and off-center framing create immediate impact.
  • Combine parameters intentionally. Expressive prompt + moderate chaos + controlled weirdness + dramatic lighting.

blocks.text: Wrapping Up
You can now:

• Design eye-catching ad visuals
  • Use chaos and weirdness with purpose
  • Guide attention through lighting and angles
  • Adapt visuals for ads and landing pages
These skills help your images perform — not just look good.

Strong editorial and social images usually aim to:

• Clarify an idea

  • Create visual rhythm across content
  • Keep the viewer reading
They rarely show the exact thing being described. Instead, they suggest, frame, or symbolize the message.

Abstract prompts sound good to humans — but they give Midjourney very little to work with. Phrases like "representing balance," "conceptual illustration," "symbolic image" don't describe a scene. Midjourney works best when it can see the metaphor, not invent it.

Instead of asking for a concept, describe a physical situation that embodies the idea. For the topic of balance, that might mean:

• Two contrasting environments or objects
  • One shared frame
  • A clear boundary or transition

blocks.text: Images That Belong to a Story

Some illustrations explain a story. Others feel like part of it. When images truly belong, they don't compete with words or summarize events. They quietly shape atmosphere, guide emotion, and help readers imagine what isn't said. This lesson will tell you how illustration choices affect immersion — and how small decisions can pull a reader closer or push them away.
One World, Many Moments

Illustrating any big long story (like a book!) means returning to the same character and world again and again.

Scenes change, emotions change, the story moves. But the reader must always feel: "I know this person. I know this place."
Scenario: Illustrating Big Volumes
Today, you're illustrating a fantasy novella. Before working on chapters, you create a single anchor image that defines:

• The main character
  • The overall visual style
  • The level of detail
This image will guide every illustration that follows.

blocks.prompt: Generate the base reference image for the story.
blocks.template: Storybook illustration of [subject] with short dark hair and a worn cloak, full height, calm observant expression, muted earthy color palette, [lighting], [style], restrained detail [aspect ratio]

blocks.text: Keeping Identity Stable

You can now pick and use one of these images as an Omni Reference. This feature helps keep the same character across chapters. It works for people, objects, or creatures. You can control how strongly the reference influences the image using --ow (Omni weight). The default value is --ow 100, and it can be from 0 to 1000.
Chapter 1: A Quiet Beginning
The story opens with a calm, reflective moment. The traveler walks alone at dawn.

blocks.prompt: Illustrate the opening scene with a stable character and gentle mood.
blocks.template: Storybook illustration of the traveler walking along an open road at dawn, soft morning mist, peaceful atmosphere, wide composition, muted colors --ar 3:2 [Omni weight] [chaos]

blocks.text: Chapter 2: Tension Builds

In the next chapter, the traveler enters a dense forest. The world feels darker, and the mood is more tense.

This is where many projects break — by changing too much at once.

blocks.prompt: Shift mood and lighting while keeping identity intact.
blocks.template: Storybook illustration of the same traveler moving through a dense forest, cooler tones, filtered light through trees, quiet tension, narrower framing --ar 3:2 [Omni weight] [chaos]

feedbackCorrect.text: Mood is different while the character is still the same!

feedbackIncorrect.text: No illustration style variations here — mood is different while the character stays the same!

blocks.question: What changed — and what stayed the same?

blocks.text: Chapter 3: Emotional Peak
Later in the story, the traveler reaches a dramatic turning point! This scene needs stronger contrast, tighter framing, and more emotional weight. But still — the same person.

blocks.prompt: Increase intensity without losing consistency.
blocks.template: Storybook illustration of the traveler standing by a campfire at night, strong contrast between warm firelight and dark surroundings, close framing, emotional intensity, painterly style --ar 3:2 [Omni weight] [chaos]

feedbackCorrect.text: As lighting, contrast, and emotional intensity increase, they start competing with the character's identity. Raising the Omni weight helps anchor the character so they remain recognizable even in more dramatic scenes.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Increasing Omni weight isn't about changing style or adding randomness. It's used to protect identity when other elements — like mood, lighting, or chaos — become stronger and could cause the character to drift.

options.label: Stronger emotion and contrast compete with identity

blocks.question: Why do you think the Omni weight was increased here?

blocks.text: The Rule You Just Discovered
As scenes become more expressive:

• Lighting grows stronger
  • Contrast increases
  • Chaos rises
You often need to slightly increase the Omni reference weight to protect identity!
From Prompts to a System
Look! You're no longer writing isolated prompts. You're reusing:

• One character reference
  • One style language
  • One prompt backbone
And making small, intentional tweaks: mood, lighting, chaos, framing. That's how books stay coherent.

• Long-form illustration starts with an anchor image: one reference that defines character, style, and detail.
  • Omni Reference keeps identity stable. Works for people, objects, or creatures across chapters.
  • --ow controls how strongly the reference holds: default 100, range 0-1000.
  • Expressive scenes compete with identity. Raise --ow slightly when lighting, contrast, or chaos increase.
  • Consistency comes from a system. Reuse one character reference, one style language, one prompt backbone.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: Illustrating at Scale
By the end of this lesson, you've learned how to:

• Anchor a character using Omni Reference
  • Control identity strength with --ow
  • Change mood without breaking style
  • Manage variation across chapters

This is the difference between generating images — and building a visual world. When readers recognize a character before they think about it, your system is working. And that's how long-form illustration succeeds.
Wrapping Up

This brings the Midjourney guide to a close.

You've moved beyond trial-and-error image generation and learned how to work with intention — shaping visuals through clear prompts, thoughtful constraints, and consistent creative systems.
You now know how to:

• Write prompts that communicate ideas, not just descriptions
  • Guide lighting, composition, and viewpoint to support a message
  • Use parameters deliberately to refine and control results
  • Apply Midjourney to different creative goals and real-world scenarios

From here, the next step is practice.

Collect your best work, experiment with longer projects, and start building a portfolio that reflects your visual thinking.

You're leaving this guide with a practical skill set and a creative framework you can return to again and again. Good luck!

blocks.text: Images That Belong to a Story

Some illustrations explain a story. Others feel like part of it. When images truly belong, they don't compete with words or summarize events. They quietly shape atmosphere, guide emotion, and help readers imagine what isn't said. This lesson will tell you how illustration choices affect immersion — and how small decisions can pull a reader closer or push them away.
One World, Many Moments

Illustrating any big long story (like a book!) means returning to the same character and world again and again.

Scenes change, emotions change, the story moves. But the reader must always feel: "I know this person. I know this place."
Scenario: Illustrating Big Volumes
Today, you're illustrating a fantasy novella. Before working on chapters, you create a single anchor image that defines:

• The main character
  • The overall visual style
  • The level of detail
This image will guide every illustration that follows.

blocks.prompt: Generate the base reference image for the story.
blocks.template: Storybook illustration of [subject] with short dark hair and a worn cloak, full height, calm observant expression, muted earthy color palette, [lighting], [style], restrained detail [aspect ratio]

blocks.text: Keeping Identity Stable

You can now pick and use one of these images as an Omni Reference. This feature helps keep the same character across chapters. It works for people, objects, or creatures. You can control how strongly the reference influences the image using --ow (Omni weight). The default value is --ow 100, and it can be from 0 to 1000.
Chapter 1: A Quiet Beginning
The story opens with a calm, reflective moment. The traveler walks alone at dawn.

blocks.prompt: Illustrate the opening scene with a stable character and gentle mood.
blocks.template: Storybook illustration of the traveler walking along an open road at dawn, soft morning mist, peaceful atmosphere, wide composition, muted colors --ar 3:2 [Omni weight] [chaos]

blocks.text: Chapter 2: Tension Builds

In the next chapter, the traveler enters a dense forest. The world feels darker, and the mood is more tense.

This is where many projects break — by changing too much at once.

blocks.prompt: Shift mood and lighting while keeping identity intact.
blocks.template: Storybook illustration of the same traveler moving through a dense forest, cooler tones, filtered light through trees, quiet tension, narrower framing --ar 3:2 [Omni weight] [chaos]

feedbackCorrect.text: Mood is different while the character is still the same!

feedbackIncorrect.text: No illustration style variations here — mood is different while the character stays the same!

blocks.question: What changed — and what stayed the same?

blocks.text: Chapter 3: Emotional Peak
Later in the story, the traveler reaches a dramatic turning point! This scene needs stronger contrast, tighter framing, and more emotional weight. But still — the same person.

blocks.prompt: Increase intensity without losing consistency.
blocks.template: Storybook illustration of the traveler standing by a campfire at night, strong contrast between warm firelight and dark surroundings, close framing, emotional intensity, painterly style --ar 3:2 [Omni weight] [chaos]

feedbackCorrect.text: As lighting, contrast, and emotional intensity increase, they start competing with the character's identity. Raising the Omni weight helps anchor the character so they remain recognizable even in more dramatic scenes.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Increasing Omni weight isn't about changing style or adding randomness. It's used to protect identity when other elements — like mood, lighting, or chaos — become stronger and could cause the character to drift.

options.label: Stronger emotion and contrast compete with identity

blocks.question: Why do you think the Omni weight was increased here?

blocks.text: The Rule You Just Discovered
As scenes become more expressive:

• Lighting grows stronger
  • Contrast increases
  • Chaos rises
You often need to slightly increase the Omni reference weight to protect identity!
From Prompts to a System
Look! You're no longer writing isolated prompts. You're reusing:

• One character reference
  • One style language
  • One prompt backbone
And making small, intentional tweaks: mood, lighting, chaos, framing. That's how books stay coherent.

• Long-form illustration starts with an anchor image: one reference that defines character, style, and detail.
  • Omni Reference keeps identity stable. Works for people, objects, or creatures across chapters.
  • --ow controls how strongly the reference holds: default 100, range 0-1000.
  • Expressive scenes compete with identity. Raise --ow slightly when lighting, contrast, or chaos increase.
  • Consistency comes from a system. Reuse one character reference, one style language, one prompt backbone.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: Illustrating at Scale
By the end of this lesson, you've learned how to:

• Anchor a character using Omni Reference
  • Control identity strength with --ow
  • Change mood without breaking style
  • Manage variation across chapters

This is the difference between generating images — and building a visual world. When readers recognize a character before they think about it, your system is working. And that's how long-form illustration succeeds.
